```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Z-Score Normalization
# • Standardizes data by centering (mean = 0) and scaling (sd = 1)
# • Useful for comparing variables with different scales
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Example data
Measurements <- c(45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70, 75)

# Perform Z-score normalization
Z_Score <- base::scale(Measurements)

# Display results
base::cbind(Measurements, Z_Score)

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Log2 Transformation
# • Reduces right-skewness and stabilizes variance
# • Commonly used in RNA-seq and proteomics data
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Example data
Measurements <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)

# Apply log2 transformation
log2Normalized <- base::log2(Measurements)

# Display results
base::cbind(Measurements, log2Normalized)

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Bonferroni Correction
# • Controls the family-wise error rate (FWER)
# • Very strict method → lowers false positives but increases false negatives
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Example p-values
p_values <- c(0.001, 0.02, 0.03, 0.15, 0.25)

# Adjust p-values using Bonferroni correction
bonferroni_p <- stats::p.adjust(p_values, method = "bonferroni")

# Display results
base::data.frame(
  Raw_p = p_values,
  Bonferroni_Adjusted_p = bonferroni_p
)

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) Correction
# • Controls the False Discovery Rate (FDR)
# • Less conservative than Bonferroni, suitable for high-throughput data
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Example p-values
p_values <- c(0.001, 0.02, 0.03, 0.15, 0.25)

# Adjust p-values using Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR) method
bh_p <- stats::p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH")

# Display results
base::data.frame(
  Raw_p = p_values,
  BH_Adjusted_p = bh_p
)

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
# • Reduces high-dimensional data into few uncorrelated components
# • Preserves most of the original variance
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Load required package
if (!requireNamespace("mixOmics", quietly = TRUE)) BiocManager::install("mixOmics")
library(mixOmics)

# Custom colors (your seminar palette)
color_palette <- c("#027375", "#e38188", "#234E70")

# Generate example data
set.seed(123)
group_labels <- rep(c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3"), each = 20)

# Create dataset with group differences across variables
data <- base::data.frame(
  Variable1 = c(stats::rnorm(20, 5, 2), stats::rnorm(20, 10, 2), stats::rnorm(20, 15, 2)),
  Variable2 = c(stats::rnorm(20, 3, 1.5), stats::rnorm(20, 7, 1.5), stats::rnorm(20, 11, 1.5)),
  Variable3 = stats::rnorm(60, 6, 2),
  Variable4 = stats::rnorm(60, 8, 3)
)
rownames(data) <- paste0("Sample_", 1:60)

# Perform PCA with mixOmics
pca_result <- mixOmics::pca(data, ncomp = 2)

# Visualize PCA
mixOmics::plotIndiv(
  pca_result,
  group = group_labels,
  legend = TRUE,
  legend.title = "Groups",
  title = "PCA: Simplified Data with Three Groups",
  pch = 16,  # Circle shape
  size.title = 14,
  size.subtitle = 12,
  size.legend = 10,
  col    = color_palette
)

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# PLS-DA with Three Groups (mixOmics)
# • Supervised dimension reduction maximizing X–Y covariance
# • Uses custom seminar palette for group colors
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Ensure mixOmics is available
if (!requireNamespace("mixOmics", quietly = TRUE)) utils::install.packages("mixOmics")

# Custom colors (your seminar palette)
color_palette <- c("#027375", "#e38188", "#234E70")

set.seed(123)
group_labels <- base::factor(rep(c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3"), each = 20))

# Simulated dataset with group differences
data <- base::data.frame(
  Var1 = c(stats::rnorm(20, 5, 2),  stats::rnorm(20, 10, 2), stats::rnorm(20, 15, 2)),
  Var2 = c(stats::rnorm(20, 3, 1.5), stats::rnorm(20, 7, 1.5), stats::rnorm(20, 11, 1.5)),
  Var3 = stats::rnorm(60, 6, 2),
  Var4 = stats::rnorm(60, 8, 3)
)
rownames(data) <- paste0("Sample_", 1:60)

# Perform PLS-DA
plsda_res <- mixOmics::plsda(data, group_labels, ncomp = 2)

# Visualize
mixOmics::plotIndiv(
  plsda_res,
  group  = group_labels,
  col    = color_palette,
  legend = TRUE,
  title  = "PLS-DA: Group Separation via Latent Components",
  pch    = 16,
  size.title  = 14,
  size.legend = 10
)

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Hierarchical Clustering (3D points → dendrogram)
# • Distance: Euclidean on x,y,z
# • Linkage: Complete (max inter-cluster distance)
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Define six points in 3D space
points_3d <- base::data.frame(
  Point = paste0("Sample_", 1:6),
  x = c(0.7, -0.5, 0.2, -0.3, 0.8, -0.7),
  y = c(0.5, -0.7, 0.3, 0.6, -0.4, 0.1),
  z = c(0.8,  0.2, -0.6, 0.1, -0.2, 0.9)
)

# Compute the distance matrix (Euclidean)
dist_matrix <- stats::dist(points_3d[, c("x", "y", "z")], method = "euclidean")

# Perform hierarchical clustering (complete linkage)
hclust_result <- stats::hclust(dist_matrix, method = "complete")

# Plot the dendrogram
graphics::plot(
  hclust_result,
  labels = points_3d$Point,
  main = "Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram",
  sub = "",
  xlab = "",
  ylab = "Distance"
)

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# K-means Clustering (2D points) + centroid visualization
# • Distance: Euclidean (default)
# • Initialization: multiple starts (nstart = 10) for stability
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Ensure ggplot2 is available
if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) utils::install.packages("ggplot2")

# Define six points in 2D space
points_2d <- base::data.frame(
  Point = paste0("Sample_", 1:6),
  x = c(0.7, -0.5, 0.2, -0.3, 0.8, -0.7),
  y = c(0.5, -0.7, 0.3, 0.6, -0.4, 0.1)
)

# Number of clusters
k <- 2L

# K-means clustering
set.seed(42)
kmeans_result <- stats::kmeans(points_2d[, c("x", "y")], centers = k, nstart = 10)

# Add cluster assignments
points_2d$Cluster <- base::as.factor(kmeans_result$cluster)

# Extract centroid coordinates
centroids <- base::as.data.frame(kmeans_result$centers)
base::colnames(centroids) <- c("x", "y")
centroids$Cluster <- base::as.factor(seq_len(k))

# Plot clustering result with centroids
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(points_2d, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, color = Cluster)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = Point), vjust = -1.5, size = 3.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = centroids, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y),
                      size = 6, shape = 4, color = "black") +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-2, 2), ylim = c(-2, 2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "K-means Clustering of Six Points",
                x = "X-axis", y = "Y-axis", color = "Cluster") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Differential Expression with limma-voom
# • Input: expression_matrix.tsv (gene + counts), pheno.tsv (sample_id, group[, batch])
# • Steps: import → align → design → voom → linear model → contrast → BH-adjusted results
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Load packages (install if missing)
if (!requireNamespace("readr", quietly = TRUE))  utils::install.packages("readr")
if (!requireNamespace("limma", quietly = TRUE))  BiocManager::install("limma")
if (!requireNamespace("edgeR", quietly = TRUE))  BiocManager::install("edgeR")
library(readr); library(limma); library(edgeR)

# 1) Load data ---------------------------------------------------------------
expr_df <- readr::read_tsv("expression_matrix.tsv")  # columns: gene, sample1, sample2, ...
pheno   <- readr::read_tsv("pheno.tsv")              # columns: sample_id, group[, batch]

# 2) Shape matrix and align columns to pheno --------------------------------
gene_ids <- expr_df$gene
expr_mat <- base::as.matrix(expr_df[, -1, drop = FALSE])
base::rownames(expr_mat) <- gene_ids

# Ensure samples match between expression matrix and pheno table
base::stopifnot(all(base::colnames(expr_mat) %in% pheno$sample_id))
pheno <- pheno[base::match(base::colnames(expr_mat), pheno$sample_id), , drop = FALSE]
base::stopifnot(base::identical(base::colnames(expr_mat), pheno$sample_id))

# 3) Design matrix -----------------------------------------------------------
pheno$group <- base::factor(pheno$group)  # ensure factor
if ("batch" %in% base::colnames(pheno)) {
  design <- stats::model.matrix(~ 0 + group + batch, data = pheno)
} else {
  design <- stats::model.matrix(~ 0 + group, data = pheno)
}
base::colnames(design) <- make.names(base::colnames(design))

# 4) voom + linear modeling --------------------------------------------------
y <- edgeR::DGEList(counts = expr_mat)
keep <- edgeR::filterByExpr(y, group = pheno$group)
y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
y <- edgeR::calcNormFactors(y, method = "TMM")

v   <- limma::voom(y, design = design, plot = FALSE)
fit <- limma::lmFit(v, design)

# 5) Contrast: last level vs first level ------------------------------------
lev <- base::levels(pheno$group)
contrast_str <- base::paste0("group", lev[2], " - group", lev[1])
cont <- limma::makeContrasts(contrasts = contrast_str, levels = design)

fit2 <- limma::contrasts.fit(fit, cont)
fit2 <- limma::eBayes(fit2, robust = TRUE, trend = TRUE)

# 6) Results -----------------------------------------------------------------
tt <- limma::topTable(fit2, coef = 1, number = Inf, sort.by = "P")
tt <- base::cbind(gene = base::rownames(tt), tt,
                  FDR = stats::p.adjust(tt$P.Value, method = "BH"))
base::rownames(tt) <- NULL

# 7) Save and quick summary --------------------------------------------------
readr::write_tsv(base::as.data.frame(tt), "limma_results.tsv")
base::print(head(tt, 10))
base::cat("Significant at FDR < 0.05:", base::sum(tt$FDR < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")

```

```{r}
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# kNN Imputation for Missing Values
# • Replaces NAs using values from the k most similar samples (rows)
# • Works best when variables are correlated; not ideal for extreme sparsity
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Install + load Bioconductor 'impute' if needed
if (!requireNamespace("impute", quietly = TRUE)) {
  if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) utils::install.packages("BiocManager")
  BiocManager::install("impute")
}
library(impute)

# Simulate data with NAs
set.seed(42)
mat <- base::matrix(stats::rnorm(50), nrow = 10)
mat[base::sample(length(mat), 5)] <- NA

# kNN imputation (k = 5)
mat_imputed <- impute::impute.knn(mat, k = 5)$data

# Quick checks
base::c(
  na_before = base::sum(base::is.na(mat)),
  na_after  = base::sum(base::is.na(mat_imputed))
)

# Visual comparison (top-left 5×5 block)
mat[1:5, 1:5]
mat_imputed[1:5, 1:5]
```
